questions.question: Which of the following best explains why the Domain Name System (DNS) is necessary in modern networking?
options: To prevent IP address conflicts on LANs
To ensure reliable packet delivery in IP networks
To dynamically allocate MAC addresses to devices
To control routing decisions across autonomous systems
To map human-readable names to IP addresses
questions.explanation:
Applications communicate using network addresses, while people and services commonly identify destinations by names. DNS supplies records that map those names to values such as IPv4 or IPv6 addresses, allowing address changes without requiring users to memorize a new number. It does not allocate MAC addresses, prevent every IP conflict, or provide reliable packet delivery.

See [Names, URLs, and the purpose of DNS](../lessons/02_dns/01_names_and_urls.md).

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why the Domain Name System (DNS) is necessary in modern networking?
options: To control routing decisions across autonomous systems
To dynamically allocate MAC addresses to devices
To map human-readable names to IP addresses
To prevent IP address conflicts on LANs
To ensure reliable packet delivery in IP networks
questions.explanation:
DNS separates the name an application uses from the address needed for IP communication. Looking up the name can return an address record, while other record types locate mail services or authoritative servers. Reliability and route selection belong to other protocols. This question duplicates Q001 with reordered options, so the correct concept is the same despite its different answer position.

See [Names, URLs, and the purpose of DNS](../lessons/02_dns/01_names_and_urls.md).

questions.question: What was a major limitation of the hosts.txt approach that motivated the development of DNS?
options: It was limited to DNSSEC-signed zones
It used TCP instead of UDP for lookups
It lacked compatibility with IPv6
It centralized control and scaled poorly
It enforced global consistency through blockchain
questions.explanation:
A single hosts.txt file required centralized administration and redistribution of an expanding name/address list. As the network grew, file size, naming conflicts, update authority, and slow propagation became difficult to manage. DNS distributes that responsibility through delegation and a hierarchy. The historical limitation was organizational and scaling-related, not dependence on DNSSEC, blockchain, or IPv6.

See [Why distributed naming and caching scale](../lessons/02_dns/02_scalable_naming.md).

questions.question: Why is aggressive caching a reasonable design choice in DNS?
options: Because DNS data is mostly read-only and loosely consistent
Because DNS records are updated more often than they are queried
Because updates are cryptographically signed
Because DNS uses TCP for most queries
Because each lookup involves every authoritative name server
questions.explanation:
DNS data is queried much more often than it changes, and many applications tolerate answers remaining unchanged for a bounded interval. Caches can therefore reuse records until their TTLs expire, saving network round trips and reducing authoritative-server work. The trade-off is delayed visibility of updates, not guaranteed immediate consistency. Cryptographic signatures can authenticate records but are not what makes caching useful.

See [Why distributed naming and caching scale](../lessons/02_dns/02_scalable_naming.md).

questions.question: Which of the following statements about recursive DNS queries is accurate?
options: Recursive queries reduce the load on local resolvers
Recursive queries are only used between root servers
Recursive queries are typically issued by authoritative name servers
Recursive queries instruct a DNS server to fully resolve a name before replying
Recursive queries are prohibited in DNSSEC deployments
questions.explanation:
A recursive query asks the receiving server to obtain a final answer or error on the client's behalf, rather than merely return its next referral. The recursive resolver may perform an iterative sequence of non-recursive queries to other servers or use cached information. RD requests this service, but a server can refuse it; recursion is not guaranteed simply because the client asks.

See [Zones, delegation, and recursive resolution](../lessons/02_dns/03_hierarchy_and_resolution.md).

questions.question: Which field in a DNS resource record determines how long the record may be cached?
options: TTL
TYPE
RDATA
CLASS
OPCODE
questions.explanation:
TTL states how long a resource record can remain usable in a cache, normally in seconds. A resolver counts down that lifetime and eventually needs fresh data for a subsequent lookup. TYPE identifies the kind of data, CLASS identifies its class, and RDATA contains the value. Those fields describe the record but do not specify its cache lifetime.

See [DNS headers and resource records](../lessons/02_dns/06_headers_and_records.md).

questions.question: What is the main role of a glue record in DNS?
options: To improve name compression efficiency
To authenticate responses from recursive resolvers
To provide an IP address for a name server within the delegated zone
To specify query retry intervals in secondary servers
To link a CNAME to its canonical name
questions.explanation:
If example.com is delegated to ns1.example.com, resolving the server's address through the child would require first reaching that same child. The parent supplies address records alongside the referral to break this circular dependency. Those bootstrap A or AAAA records act as glue; glue is not a distinct record type or a cryptographic authentication mechanism.

See [Bootstrapping, glue, and delegation inspection](../lessons/02_dns/04_root_hints_and_glue.md).

questions.question: Which section of a DNS reply contains glue records?
options: Additional
Question
Header
Answer
Authority
questions.explanation:
A referral normally places the child-zone NS records in Authority and useful address records for those servers in Additional. In-bailiwick bootstrap addresses in Additional can therefore serve as glue. Not every Additional record is glue, and a referral need not contain the final requested answer. The section roles matter more than simply whether the response has any records.

See [DNS transport and message sections](../lessons/02_dns/05_transport_and_sections.md); [Bootstrapping, glue, and delegation inspection](../lessons/02_dns/04_root_hints_and_glue.md).

questions.question: What does the RD (recursion desired) bit in a DNS header indicate?
options: That the response is from a root server
That this is an authoritative answer
That the client requests the server to perform recursion
That the query is signed with DNSSEC
That the server is using TCP instead of UDP
questions.explanation:
RD means recursion desired: the requester wants the server to resolve the question fully on its behalf. RA is the separate indication that recursion is available, and AA indicates an authoritative answer. Setting RD does not prove the server offers recursion, make the response authoritative, or enable DNSSEC or TCP.

See [DNS headers and resource records](../lessons/02_dns/06_headers_and_records.md).

questions.question: In DNS message compression, what does a label starting with bits '11' (e.g., 0xC0) represent?
options: A negative response for NXDOMAIN
A truncated answer due to UDP limit
A compressed TXT record
A pointer to a previously encoded domain name
An indicator of an authoritative name server
questions.explanation:
When the top two bits are 11, the two-byte encoding is a compression pointer rather than an ordinary length-prefixed label. Its remaining 14 bits identify an offset to a previously encoded name or suffix in the same DNS message. The first byte need not equal exactly 0xC0. Reusing a suffix saves space without changing the name's meaning.

See [Labels, name encoding, and compression](../lessons/02_dns/07_names_and_compression.md).

questions.question: Which SOA record field controls how often a secondary server checks for zone updates?
options: Retry
Refresh
Minimum TTL
Expire
Serial Number
questions.explanation:
The SOA refresh interval tells a secondary how often to check for an updated zone. The serial identifies the version, retry governs another attempt after a failed check, and expire limits service without successful refresh. These are replication controls, distinct from the TTL controlling how long a recursive resolver can reuse an ordinary cached record.

See [Replication, SOA, and cache lifetimes](../lessons/02_dns/08_replication_and_caching.md).

questions.question: What is a key consequence of using a CNAME record in DNS?
options: It requires an extra lookup to resolve the canonical name
It blocks DNSSEC validation for the original domain
It prevents the use of additional sections in replies
It eliminates the need for zone file delegation
It allows multiple IPs for a single name without A records
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** A CNAME tells the resolver to follow another name to obtain the requested ordinary data, so it adds name indirection. That need not require an additional network lookup: the reply may already contain the target's address, or the address may be cached. The preserved key overstates this as an unavoidable extra lookup. CNAME following is also different from an HTTP redirect or an NS delegation.

See [CNAME chains and alias restrictions](../lessons/02_dns/09_aliases_and_cname.md).

questions.question: Which DNS server type typically provides the location of a TLD server when resolving a domain name?
options: Forwarding proxy
Authoritative server
Recursive resolver
Stub resolver
Root server
questions.explanation:
Starting without a usable cached referral, a recursive resolver can ask a root server and receive the relevant TLD's name-server information. It then asks the TLD and follows further delegation toward the authoritative zone. The root provides the top-level referral rather than resolving every host itself. Cached referrals can let later queries bypass this initial step.

See [Zones, delegation, and recursive resolution](../lessons/02_dns/03_hierarchy_and_resolution.md).

questions.question: What happens when a DNS query receives an NXDOMAIN response?
options: The domain is permanently blacklisted by the resolver
The resolver retries using TCP instead of UDP
The resolver generates a REFUSED status for future queries
The result is cached for the TTL specified in the SOA’s minimum field
The response is forwarded to a higher-level authoritative server
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** NXDOMAIN says the queried name does not exist and can be cached as a negative result. Its negative-cache lifetime is bounded by the lesser of SOA.MINIMUM and the SOA record's own TTL, not MINIMUM alone as the preserved key suggests. For MINIMUM=900 and an SOA TTL of 300 seconds, the starting lifetime is at most 300 seconds. This is temporary caching, not permanent blacklisting.

See [Replication, SOA, and cache lifetimes](../lessons/02_dns/08_replication_and_caching.md).

questions.question: If a zone includes a wildcard record *.example.com, what happens when a query for unknown.example.com is made?
options: The wildcard generates a synthetic answer
The query triggers a fallback to the root zone
The query is redirected using a glue record
The query is rewritten using the original zone apex
The query always fails with NXDOMAIN

questions.question: How does DNS implement basic load balancing using A records?
options: By ordering multiple A records and rotating them in responses
By assigning each user to a unique resolver
By issuing TCP resets to distribute query load
By delegating each query to a random authoritative server
By hashing the client’s IP to select a response path
questions.explanation:
A name can return several A records, and the server or resolver can vary their order across replies. Clients that try different first entries can spread connections across the corresponding servers. This is basic round-robin distribution, not a guarantee of equal load or backend health. Client selection, caching, and connection reuse influence the actual result.

See [Round-robin DNS and address selection](../lessons/02_dns/12_load_balancing.md).

questions.question: What is a practical impact of setting a very long TTL on DNS records?
options: It increases DNSSEC validation overhead
It guarantees frequent updates from authoritative servers
It causes authoritative servers to ignore refresh requests
It disables client-side caching
It reduces DNS lookup latency but slows update propagation
questions.explanation:
A long TTL allows a resolver to reuse an answer for longer, reducing repeat lookups and often their latency and server load. The same lifetime lets an old answer persist after the authoritative data changes, delaying what clients observe. This affects cached answers; it does not force authoritative servers to ignore secondary refresh or guarantee an immediate update everywhere.

See [Replication, SOA, and cache lifetimes](../lessons/02_dns/08_replication_and_caching.md).

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a DNS delegation?
options: The act of forwarding a query through NAT
The process of caching answers at a recursive resolver
The replication of data between secondary servers
The dynamic update of resource records from DHCP
The linking of a parent zone to a child zone's name server
questions.explanation:
A parent delegates a child zone by publishing NS information identifying the child's authoritative servers. That passes administrative responsibility for the delegated portion of the namespace while giving resolvers a route toward its answers. Delegation is not simply caching, copying a primary zone to a secondary, or forwarding a query through NAT.

See [Zones, delegation, and recursive resolution](../lessons/02_dns/03_hierarchy_and_resolution.md).

questions.question: What makes DNS cache poisoning a viable attack vector?
options: DNS responses can be spoofed if the transaction ID is predicted
DNS queries are always encrypted end-to-end
DNSSEC always validates CNAME records only
Authoritative servers enforce TTL constraints
Recursive resolvers ignore glue records
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** An attacker can poison a cache by racing a legitimate reply with a forged response that the resolver accepts. Predicting the transaction ID helps, but the response must also match relevant addresses, ports, and the question; ID prediction alone is insufficient. Those matching checks raise the difficulty of forgery without providing cryptographic data-origin authentication. A poisoned cached answer can then affect later clients.

See [Forgery and cache poisoning](../lessons/02_dns/13_forgery_and_cache_poisoning.md).

questions.question: What problem is DNSSEC primarily designed to solve?
options: Provide authenticity and integrity of DNS data
Prevent recursive queries to root servers
Reduce latency by enforcing client caching
Eliminate the need for glue records
Guarantee authoritative servers are online
questions.explanation:
DNSSEC uses signed RRsets and a chain of trusted keys to let a validating resolver check DNS data's authenticity and integrity. It does not encrypt the records or guarantee that the authoritative server remains available. Signing and validation are separate deployment choices, so a signature helps clients only when the relevant trust chain is established and checked.

See [DNSSEC data authentication and deployment](../lessons/02_dns/14_dnssec.md).

questions.question: What is the role of a Delegation Signer (DS) record in DNSSEC?
options: It replaces NS records for child zones
It signals that caching should be disabled for a zone
It encrypts the query payload for confidentiality
It carries a hashed public key of the child zone
It serves as a backup TTL in case of RRSIG expiration
questions.explanation:
A DS record in the parent contains a digest identifying a child zone's DNSKEY. Once the parent's data is authenticated, the resolver can check that the child's key matches that digest and continue validating the child's signatures. DS links trust across a delegation; it neither replaces NS reachability information nor encrypts the query payload.

See [DNSSEC data authentication and deployment](../lessons/02_dns/14_dnssec.md).

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes DNS redirection from HTTP redirection?
options: HTTP redirection can change the URL shown to the user, unlike DNS redirection
HTTP redirection relies on recursive resolvers to modify records
DNS redirection requires browser cookie support
DNS redirection is only used in load balancing while HTTP redirection is not
DNS redirection works at the application layer using TCP

questions.question: What does a recursive resolver do when a cached DNS entry's TTL has expired?
options: Increases TTL to prevent overloading name servers
Blocks all queries for the corresponding domain
Returns a REFUSED error to the client
Forwards the expired answer with a warning
Drops the record and re-queries the authoritative server
questions.explanation:
In the ordinary TTL model, an expired cached record cannot be reused as a fresh cache hit. When another request needs that data, the resolver obtains a fresh answer, following any still-usable cached referrals toward an authority. Expiry alone need not trigger an immediate background query or a new root lookup. The lesson does not cover special policies for serving stale answers.

See [Replication, SOA, and cache lifetimes](../lessons/02_dns/08_replication_and_caching.md).

questions.question: Why does DNS use UDP for most of its queries?
options: UDP allows encryption and compression by default
TCP is not supported by most recursive resolvers
TCP requires DNSSEC, which is rarely used
UDP supports longer queries than TCP
UDP reduces latency due to its connectionless nature
questions.explanation:
UDP can carry a simple DNS request and response without first establishing a stream connection, avoiding that setup cost for a short exchange. DNS also supports TCP, including responses that cannot be delivered adequately over the chosen UDP exchange. UDP does not supply encryption by default, and its use is not evidence that TCP or DNSSEC is unsupported.

See [DNS transport and message sections](../lessons/02_dns/05_transport_and_sections.md).

questions.question: What event causes a DNS client to retry the query using TCP instead of UDP?
options: The SOA record is unsigned
The AA bit is missing from the response
The response contains a wildcard record
The RD bit is set to 0
The response includes the TC (truncated) flag
questions.explanation:
TC indicates that a DNS response was truncated. A client can retry over TCP to obtain a complete response, with DNS messages framed by a two-byte length on the TCP byte stream. The original unextended UDP DNS size limit was 512 bytes; EDNS can permit larger UDP payloads. AA and RD describe different properties and do not themselves signal truncation.

See [DNS transport and message sections](../lessons/02_dns/05_transport_and_sections.md).

questions.question: What makes DNS susceptible to amplification attacks?
options: It allows unauthenticated updates to zone files
It requires frequent refresh of negative caches
It uses TCP which supports session hijacking
Zone transfers are broadcast to all root servers
A small query can trigger a large response from an open resolver

questions.question: What is a key benefit of using DNS over HTTPS (DoH) or DNS over TLS (DoT)?
options: It encrypts DNS queries to prevent eavesdropping
It guarantees DNSSEC validation at the client
It replaces the need for recursive resolution entirely
It reduces the size of DNS packets using compression
It eliminates the need for authoritative name servers
questions.explanation:
DoH and DoT encrypt the client-to-resolver transport, reducing what on-path observers can learn from DNS message contents on that connection. The receiving resolver still sees the query so it can answer it. Encrypted transport does not itself validate the DNSSEC chain or automatically protect every subsequent resolver-to-authoritative exchange; confidentiality and data authentication are separate concerns.

See [Encrypted DNS and resolver trust](../lessons/02_dns/16_encrypted_dns.md).

questions.question: What is a major privacy concern with using a public recursive DNS resolver?
options: It caches records for longer TTLs than private resolvers
It can log and profile client queries without consent
It disables caching to preserve consistency
It forces all queries to be recursive
It must run on the same subnet as the client
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** A public recursive resolver receives the names its clients ask about and can potentially log or analyze those queries. Encrypting the connection does not hide the query from that endpoint. Whether a particular provider profiles users or acts without consent depends on its policy and behavior, not a required property of public DNS. The preserved key should be read as a possible privacy risk, not a universal claim.

See [Encrypted DNS and resolver trust](../lessons/02_dns/16_encrypted_dns.md).

questions.question: What is the function of a stub resolver in DNS resolution?
options: It sends queries to a recursive resolver on behalf of an application
It modifies TTLs to match local caching policies
It performs full recursive resolution without external help
It maintains the authoritative records for its domain
It stores glue records for local name servers
questions.explanation:
The stub resolver is the client-side component that asks a recursive resolver a DNS question for an application. It delegates the wider search rather than normally walking root, TLD, and authoritative referrals itself. A configured naming interface may also consult local sources, but a stub is not the authoritative database for the domain it queries.

See [Zones, delegation, and recursive resolution](../lessons/02_dns/03_hierarchy_and_resolution.md).

questions.question: What does Dynamic DNS (DDNS) enable in conjunction with DHCP?
options: Preloading all authoritative records into stub resolvers
Real-time updates of DNS records when IPs are assigned
Conversion of MAC addresses into domain names
Client-side certificate validation for recursive resolvers
Replacing the DNS hierarchy with flat namespaces

questions.question: What is the function of the DNS root zone in the overall hierarchy?
options: It issues wildcard certificates for secure DNS
It replicates zone files to recursive resolvers
It stores the IPs of all authoritative servers globally
It delegates queries to appropriate top-level domain (TLD) servers
It resolves all queries involving CNAME chains
questions.explanation:
The root zone supplies delegations toward top-level domains such as .com or .se. A resolver uses the corresponding name-server information to continue down the hierarchy toward the requested zone. The root does not maintain the address of every host or complete every CNAME chain; delegation distributes both the search and administrative responsibility.

See [Zones, delegation, and recursive resolution](../lessons/02_dns/03_hierarchy_and_resolution.md).
